Empirical Research Plan: “Shared Stock- and Bond-Market Risk Factors”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Linear multifactor asset–pricing tests implemented with the
Fama-MacBeth two–step procedure and GMM‐based specification tests.

Rationale
• The question is not about the causal impact of an intervention; it is
about whether a parsimonious set of systematic factors can *explain the
cross-section of average returns*.  
• The appropriate “identification” is therefore to recover the risk
prices (λ’s) in the linear factor model  

       E[R_i] = β_i′ λ                      (*i* = test asset)

and to test whether the model’s pricing errors (α_i) are jointly zero.
• Fama-MacBeth delivers unbiased risk-price estimates under classical
measurement error in estimated betas and allows straightforward
inference with the Shanken correction.  A system-GMM or
Hansen–Jagannathan distance minimisation gives an over-identifying
restriction test.

Because the goal is to evaluate whether the candidate factors span the
stochastic discount factor, “other” (factor-model estimation) is the
only conceptually coherent strategy; DID, IV, RDD, or event studies are
not suited to this question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Although there is no “treatment” in the policy sense, we can cast the
exercise in treatment-control language to satisfy the template:

• Treatment variable  
  – Continuous: the *ex-ante* loading (β) of a portfolio on a given
    factor, estimated from a rolling 60-month time-series regression.

• Treated units  
  – Portfolios whose β on that factor lies in the top tercile.

• Control units  
  – Portfolios in the bottom tercile of that β distribution.

• Timing  
  – β’s are formed at the end of month *t–1* using returns *t–60 … t–1*.
    Average returns in month *t* are the outcome.

This framing allows us to interpret factor risk as the “treatment
intensity,” with low-β portfolios serving as counterfactuals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Linear factor structure  
    True expected returns are linear in betas on the candidate factors.

A2. Constant factor loadings within the estimation window  
    β_i,t is stable over the 60-month window used to estimate it.

A3. Factors are correctly measured and tradable  
    Observed factor-mimicking portfolios proxy perfectly for the true
    common shocks.

A4. No omitted priced factors  
    Any omitted factor is either uncorrelated with included betas or is
    not priced.

A5. Idiosyncratic returns are mean-zero and uncorrelated with factors  
    E[ε_i|F] = 0.

Plausibility
• Decades of evidence support approximate linear factor structures in
  equity and fixed-income markets; the chosen factors (MKT, SMB, HML,
  TERM, DEF) have strong theoretical backing.  
• Using 60-month windows is standard and balances precision with the
  possibility of time-variation in betas.  
• The factors are tradable portfolios constructed from publicly
  available returns, so measurement error is likely classical, though
  not zero.  
• Omitted factors are the main worry; we handle this in Section 4.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Measurement error in β’s  
    • Mitigation: Shanken (1992) correction of the F-statistic; use
      errors-in-variables IV approach that instruments β_i with the same
      β’s estimated on a *non-overlapping* sub-sample.

T2. Omitted systematic factors (model mis-specification)  
    • Mitigation: Conduct specification tests (Hansen-Jagannathan,
      Gibbons-Ross-Shanken) and augment the model with additional
      candidates (e.g., momentum, liquidity) as robustness.  
    • Run principal-component analysis on residuals to detect missing
      common structure.

T3. Time-variation in risk prices or betas  
    • Mitigation: Allow λ_t to vary by estimating rolling 10-year
      Fama-MacBeth regressions and test parameter stability; interact
      betas with NBER recession dummies.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)         # fast OLS
library(zoo)            # rolling windows
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov
library(lmtest)
library(purrr)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
# Assume five CSV files in working directory
#------------------------------------------------------------
ret_stk  <- read_csv("25_stock_portfolios.csv")   # cols: date, p1, p2, ...
ret_gov  <- read_csv("gov_bond_portfolios.csv")   # cols: date, 1y, 5y, 10y
ret_cor  <- read_csv("corp_bond_portfolios.csv")  # cols: date, Aaa, Baa, ...
factors  <- read_csv("factor_returns.csv")        # date, MKT, SMB, HML, TERM, DEF
rf       <- read_csv("risk_free.csv")             # date, rf

# Merge all
dat <- list(ret_stk, ret_gov, ret_cor, factors, rf) %>%
  reduce(full_join, by = "date") %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(across(-date, ~ .x - rf$rf))             # excess returns

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Estimate betas with 60-month rolling window
#------------------------------------------------------------
roll_beta <- function(ret_vec, factors_mat){
  rollapplyr(
    data = cbind(ret_vec, factors_mat),
    width = 60,
    FUN = function(x){
      y <- x[,1]; X <- x[,-1]
      coef(lm(y ~ X))[-1]                           # drops intercept
    },
    by.column = FALSE, align = "right", fill = NA)
}

factor_names <- c("MKT","SMB","HML","TERM","DEF")
X <- dat %>% select(all_of(factor_names)) %>% as.matrix()

beta_list <- dat %>%
  select(-date, -all_of(factor_names)) %>%
  map(~ roll_beta(.x, X))                          # returns list of matrices

# Convert list to long tibble
beta_df <- imap_dfr(beta_list, ~ as_tibble(.x) %>%
                      mutate(date = dat$date,
                             asset = .y)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(date, asset),
               names_to = "factor", values_to = "beta")

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Fama-MacBeth second step
#------------------------------------------------------------
# Average returns over full sample
mean_ret <- dat %>%
  select(-all_of(factor_names)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "asset", values_to = "ret") %>%
  group_by(asset) %>%
  summarise(E_R = mean(ret, na.rm = TRUE))

# Merge betas and expected returns
cs_data <- beta_df %>%
  group_by(asset, factor) %>%
  summarise(beta = mean(beta, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = factor, values_from = beta) %>%
  left_join(mean_ret, by = "asset")

# Cross-sectional regression
fm_eq <- as.formula(paste("E_R ~", paste(factor_names, collapse = " + ")))
fm_est <- feols(fm_eq, data = cs_data, se = "hetero")

summary(fm_est)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Specification test: Gibbons-Ross-Shanken
#------------------------------------------------------------
# Time-series alpha for each asset
get_alpha <- function(ret, betas, lambda_hat){
  mean(ret, na.rm = TRUE) - as.numeric(betas %*% lambda_hat)
}

lambda_hat <- coef(fm_est)[factor_names]

alphas <- cs_data %>%
  mutate(alpha = get_alpha(E_R, as.matrix(select(., all_of(factor_names))),
                           lambda_hat))

# GRS statistic (simple version)
Sigma <- dat %>%
  select(-all_of(factor_names)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "asset", values_to = "ret") %>%
  group_by(asset) %>%
  summarise(var = var(ret, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(var) %>%
  diag()

GRS_num <- nrow(alphas) * t(alphas$alpha) %*% solve(Sigma) %*% alphas$alpha
GRS_den <- 1 + t(lambda_hat) %*% solve(cov(dat[,factor_names])) %*% lambda_hat
GRS_stat <- as.numeric(GRS_num / GRS_den) / length(factor_names)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Add momentum factor
#------------------------------------------------------------
factors <- factors %>% mutate(WML = read_csv("momentum.csv")$WML)
factor_names2 <- c(factor_names, "WML")
# repeat steps with expanded factor set ...
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior based on the literature (annualised risk premia)

• λ_MKT  ≈ 6–8 %  
• λ_SMB  ≈ 2–3 %  
• λ_HML  ≈ 4–5 %  
• λ_TERM ≈ 2–3 %  
• λ_DEF  ≈ 1 %  

I expect:
1. All five λ’s positive and jointly significant.  
2. Pricing errors (α’s) for both stock and bond portfolios small and
   statistically indistinguishable from zero, indicating that the
   shared factor structure is adequate.  
3. Omitting TERM and DEF should leave sizeable, systematic α’s for bond
   portfolios, while omitting SMB and HML should leave pricing errors
   for small-growth vs. value stocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = yes, 0 = doubt)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Factors theoretically motivated and tradable ............... 1  
C2: β’s precisely estimated (60-month window, portfolios) ....... 1  
C3: No important omitted factors ................................ 0  
C4: Time-invariance of λ’s over sample .......................... 0  
C5: Robust inference (Shanken, GRS, sub-periods) ............... 1  

Total = 3 / 5.  Main concerns are potential omitted factors and
time-variation in prices of risk, which the robustness checks will
probe but cannot fully rule out.
